A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DBALD research work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable and matchable. v2 includes Appendices A–E; v1 ends after its references without appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on four lane detectors using CULane and TuSimple, including ablations, physical attacks, and defense evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds loss ablations, cross-model transfer results, false-positive measurements, and physical mud-trigger tests.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix B.6 add explicit LPIPS-based filtering of generated triggers against benign-pattern and poisoned-trigger databases. This extends the specified trigger-selection procedure, while the heatmap search, diffusion update, and two generation losses remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun with this filtering.

E1.justification: CULane, TuSimple, and the three lane-attack tasks remain unchanged. Appendix E.2 extends physical evaluation to actual mud triggers, previously evaluated digitally; v1's physical experiments used cones. The additional cone visualizations cover the existing four road environments.

E2.justification: The evaluated attack baselines, forensic detectors, and defense methods remain the same. Both versions explicitly identify the anomaly detector as Qwen2.5-VL; v2's inconsistent Qwen3-VL reference does not establish an evaluated-model substitution.

E3.justification: Added evaluations introduce separate removal of each diffusion loss, LaneATT-to-RESA heatmap transfer, benign-data false-positive measurement, and a 50-sample physical mud test. Existing benchmark metrics, poisoning rate, trigger sizes, and attack parameters remain unchanged. The newly stated ResNet-34 backbone is additional disclosure, not an established configuration change.

E4.justification: v2 substantially broadens validation through quantitative ablations separating the two diffusion losses, cross-model transfer analysis, false-positive analysis, and additional model-specific heatmap and physical case studies. Existing illumination, trigger-size, poisoning-rate, and attention-concentration analyses largely move into Appendix B rather than being newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both primarily report point estimates; averages across attack strategies are not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: New results include loss-ablation detection scores of 2.46/12.13/14.51, transfer ASR of 71.49%, reported benign-data false-positive rate of 8.2%, and physical-mud ASR of 62% on 50 samples. Table 1 revises LaneATT/CULane average ASR from 77.23 to 76.41 without changing its component scores. Clean-model accuracies on poisoned inputs and most detailed pruning results are removed; the main comparative scores otherwise remain stable.

T1.justification: The formal attack definitions, threat assumptions, gradient-map equation, diffusion recurrence, and generation-loss formulas remain unchanged. Appendices A and D expand explanations without adding proofs, theorems, or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: attention-guided placement, diffusion-generated naturalistic triggers, dual consistency losses, and effectiveness across digital and physical settings. The headline 10.87% ASR improvement and 56.59% stealthiness improvement claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges minor clean-accuracy degradation instead of claiming none, discusses unavoidable false positives and evaluation with only two trigger instances, and interprets transfer results as evidence of partly model-independent vulnerabilities. It also adds explanations connecting low-light clean accuracy to trigger sensitivity and treating generation overhead as acceptable for offline poisoning.

D1.justification: v2 materially expands implementation documentation: a shared ResNet-34 backbone, detailed detector heads and losses, backpropagation through denoising, LPIPS filtering with a 0.15 threshold and reference-database construction, and generation time of six seconds per image versus one second for baselines. These are substantial disclosures, without establishing corresponding changes to previously used settings.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on 6D-pose and video-segmentation backdoors, perceptual metrics, and quantization-related defense, while removing PEFTGuard and several lane-detection and image-editing references. Its positioning against LD-Attack and BadLane and its diffusion-for-lane-detection novelty claim remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work and contribution explanations are condensed, the explicit research-question framing is removed, evaluation passages are rewritten, and several analyses move into newly organized Appendices A–E. Author affiliations and section headings also change.

P2.justification: v2 restructures Table 1, relocates several analysis tables and the trigger-size plot to appendices, removes v1's direct stealthiness-comparison figure and full pruning table, and adds a loss-selection table, a model-by-strategy heatmap grid, and a larger physical-scene montage. These substantially change the presentation beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: Separate loss ablations, transfer testing, physical mud results, and fuller implementation disclosures modestly strengthen the paper's support and reproducibility. The gains are limited by incomplete specifications for some new evaluations and the removal of detailed pruning results and the direct visual stealthiness comparison. The principal benchmark evidence and conclusions remain largely unchanged.
